cells.tense: The pen stays down on the practice that has earned its place.
cells.ask: Take one hour off from the practice this week, on purpose, and write down whether you missed it or only felt behind.
cells.core:
You keep one practice going and you know why it's still there, which is rarer than the fact that you keep it. When a session is missed or a week turns poor, that doesn't sway it either way. You pick it up again because it's yours, not because you're being watched. Some weeks the room does nearly all the work and your part is just to show up. What you drop tends to be the part that was only ever tolerable, which is how the hours you do give have this much behind them.

That care is what the practice can feed next. It can widen into the other tending you've left on the shelf while this one got all the attention. So let one hour go dark this week: no leaning into the practice to recover the time, no extra minutes the next day as penance. Then write whether you missed the hour itself or just the ticking box. Either answer is useful.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it because it's chosen, not because it's enforced.
cells.verb: keeping the chosen practice under real conditions, and properly ending what doesn't hold
cells.place: a clearing made by opening your grip

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead is the session where it finally proves itself, and you are already living there.
cells.ask: Set a timer and stop the session when it rings, mid-set mid-line, before it feels finished or good.
cells.core:
You are pushing the practice past what it can carry. The repeat, the extra round, the next block of weeks — each one aimed at the version ahead, where the work finally shows and you get credit and nothing slips. You read a bad day as proof the method is wrong and keep casting around for the one that isn't. The ordinary session in front of you keeps getting treated as a rehearsal for the real one; the grip has moved off the practice and onto the outcome it's supposed to deliver.

What usually sets a practice in place for you is a clean stop, not another grind. So set a timer, and when it rings, stop right there — mid-set, mid-line, before it feels finished or good. Ten minutes of closing counts. Ending on purpose shows you what you are really giving the practice and what the practice is for.
cells.sheetLine: When you stop mid-set, you show yourself nothing is chasing you.
cells.verb: keeping the chosen practice under real conditions, and properly ending what doesn't hold
cells.place: a clearing made by opening your grip

cells.tense: A test came through and the practice never got restored after it.
cells.ask: Do ten minutes of the practice tomorrow, not to catch up or make it good, just to test whether the door is still there.
cells.core:
You know what it is to keep something and one day wake up set down on the other side of it. The shelf, the mat, the file — the tools of something you were committed to, now out of use. There isn't more resolve in you to keep something running; there is the fact of a practice that stopped when the going got hard or the world got loud, and a place you used to stand that you no longer stand in. Nothing here is wrong with you. Something small stopped being fed and went quiet.

You don't need a plan to reopen it. Put in ten minutes tomorrow, in whatever form is within reach, and do it badly. Not to catch up, not to make it good. The point is to find out whether the door is still there. The first minutes back rarely feel like anything; the practice trusts returning more than it rewards a good day.
cells.sheetLine: Doing it badly tomorrow tells you more than planning it well.

cells.tense: You have already cleared room for what matters and you keep calling it a lack of time.
cells.ask: Name one thing you dropped because it wasn't worth the upkeep, then keep the space open for a week without refilling it.
cells.core:
You are going through the practice as though the value only arrives later. Once the streak holds, once you've earned the right to stop proving, then it counts as something you chose. Meanwhile you are already shaped by it, and already letting things go — the tone in your voice, the hour you go back to, the offer let go of because it wasn't worth the upkeep. You call those just how things are, not choices you made.

What you've let go has been standing there for a while. Name one of those dropped commitments and leave the space open for a week without filling it with the next thing. Doing that shows you the shaping you've been doing, so it can start coming from you on purpose.
cells.sheetLine: The space you cleared happened first. Now you can name it.

attempts.check: The likely unsupported claim is that this practice has a steady outside reason behind it; the record only gives the capacity and its aim, not the person's history, and the reader could rightly say the reason has drained and nothing else is holding it. The ask survives the read being wrong because it is one reachable fact outside the practice, worth naming whether or not commitment is the issue. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about what the practice is quietly costing; I have cut that and left the cost in the ask.
